Addressed to the **BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026**.

# Project Overview

This project will use two datasets already recommended in the BST260 project materials. I will combine descriptive statistics, visualization, and introductory linear models to study two associations without interpreting either as causal. The first study will examine physical activity and measured pulse rate in young adults. The second will examine seasonal patterns across water-exposure types in reported waterborne outbreaks. Both studies will document data provenance, missingness, and limitations before any formal analysis is interpreted.

# Study 1: Physical Activity and Measured Pulse Rate in Young Adults

## Research Question and Motivation

Among adults aged 19--40, how are participation in moderate or vigorous physical activity and weekly activity frequency associated with measured pulse rate? I expect participants who report physical activity to have lower average pulse rates than inactive participants, and I expect more activity days among active participants to be associated with lower pulse rates. These are prespecified hypotheses rather than preliminary findings. A systematic review of interventional studies found that exercise, particularly endurance training, can reduce resting heart rate, which provides a motivation for examining a related association in this educational dataset (Reimers, Knapp, & Reimers, 2018).

## Data Source and Study Population

I will use the educational `NHANES` data frame from the [`NHANES` R package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/NHANES/refman/NHANES.html). It combines the 2009--2010 and 2011--2012 survey cycles and contains a resampled version of the original NHANES data. The package documentation states that the educational `NHANES` data contain 10,000 rows resampled from 20,293 rows of `NHANESraw` to reduce the effects of oversampling, and warns that the result is not a research database. The unit of analysis will be an individual record for a participant aged 19--40, inclusive. Because resampling can produce repeated participant IDs, I will report both the number of records and the number of unique IDs, inspect the multiplicities, and avoid arbitrary deduplication. Inferential results will therefore be presented as educational associations with appropriate caution.

## Exposure, Outcome, and Covariates

The primary binary exposure will be `PhysActive`, defined as whether the participant reports moderate- or vigorous-intensity sports, fitness, or recreational activity. Among participants with a valid active response, the secondary exposure will be `PhysActiveDays`, the reported number of activity days in a typical week. The outcome will be `Pulse`, documented by the package as a 60-second pulse rate. I will call this a measured pulse rate rather than assume that it is a strictly standardized resting heart rate.

The primary adjustment set will be age, `Sex`, and `Race1`, selected from subject-matter reasoning before examining associations. I will consider `BMI` and `Smoke100` in sensitivity analyses. BMI may partly lie on a pathway between activity and pulse, so it will not be treated as an automatic primary confounder. `Smoke100` is only reported for participants aged 20 years or older, so any analysis using it will use an explicitly defined age-restricted sensitivity sample.

## Missing Data and Planned Analysis

I will describe sample size, mean, median, standard deviation, IQR, and missingness for every analysis variable. I will distinguish the structural non-applicability of `PhysActiveDays` for participants who do not report activity from a missing response among active participants; I will not recode all missing activity days to zero. The main frequency analysis will be restricted to active participants with valid frequency measurements. The primary analysis will use a documented complete-case rule and will discuss possible selection bias.

Planned displays include boxplots of measured pulse rate by `PhysActive` and a plot of pulse rate against activity days. I will fit an unadjusted linear model and a multiple linear model adjusted for age, sex, and race, reporting estimated associations and confidence intervals. A physical-activity-by-sex interaction will be a secondary analysis rather than a data-driven subgroup search. BMI and smoking will be added only as sensitivity analyses, and I will check whether the available survey cycles support the same variable definitions before combining them.

## Potential Limitations

The data are cross-sectional, activity is self-reported, and the pulse measurement may not represent a laboratory-defined resting heart rate. Complete-case analysis may select a different population from the target age group. The educational resampling scheme and repeated IDs also limit ordinary survey inference. Results will be described as associations and will not be used to claim that exercise causes a lower pulse rate.

# Study 2: Seasonal Patterns in Waterborne Illness Data

## Research Question and Motivation

Among reported waterborne outbreaks with a known water-exposure type, how do the four-season distributions differ between drinking-water and recreational-water outbreaks, and do these patterns vary across reporting decades? Comparing all four seasons preserves information that would be lost by reducing the outcome to summer versus non-summer. The season will be based on the recorded month: winter will include December through February, spring March through May, summer June through August, and autumn September through November.

## Data Source, Unit, and Exposure

I will use the `waterborne` object included in this package. It was retrieved from the CDC open-data endpoint described in the package documentation and demonstrated in the BST260 [CDC API lecture](https://vjcitn.github.io/2026vjc/slides/prob/20-sep23-cards-cdc.html). The original object is a nested list rather than a rectangular data frame. The unit of analysis will be one reported outbreak.

The primary exposure will be a two-level variable created from the observed `water_exposure` labels: `Drinking water` versus `Recreational water`, with treated and untreated recreational-water labels combined. Records with mixed, undetermined, other/environmental, or missing exposure labels will not be silently assigned to either group. I will report how many records are excluded from the primary comparison and retain them in the data audit. A secondary analysis will keep treated and untreated recreational-water records separate if their sample sizes support a stable comparison. This definition keeps the main comparison interpretable while respecting the source data.

## Outcome, Covariates, and Missing Data

The primary outcome will be a four-level season variable derived from the recorded `month` field after validating its character-to-integer conversion. Calendar decade and geographic region are potential covariates because surveillance practices, reporting systems, and the distribution of water settings may change over time and across regions. I will derive a region from state when a standard state mapping is available and document how territories, multistate records, and unmatched locations are handled. The number of reported illnesses will be retained as a secondary descriptive measure rather than used to define the main outcome.

## Planned Analysis and Limitations

I will convert the nested list to a tidy data frame, create the four-season variable, and summarize seasonal counts and proportions by exposure group. Stacked bar charts and heatmaps will show the seasonal distribution, first overall and then by reporting decade. The primary comparison will retain all eligible outbreaks with valid month and exposure values. If the data support it, I will fit a simple model or estimate adjusted contrasts including reporting decade and region; I will avoid unnecessary pairwise testing across seasons. I will also write a reusable R function for grouped seasonal summaries. Outbreak size and the largest 1% of events may be shown as secondary descriptive checks, but genuine extreme events will not be removed from the primary seasonal analysis.

The dataset may reflect reporting bias, missing outbreak characteristics, reporting delays, and changes in surveillance over time. The recorded month may not be the month in which exposure occurred, and the number of reports is not a population-level incidence measure because exposure denominators are unavailable. The analysis will therefore remain descriptive or associational and cannot establish that water-exposure type causes a particular seasonal pattern.
